rashi:a1.1: And all of them who retracted: this is the end of the baraita above, which teaches: One who comes to accept the matters of ḥaver status except for one thing, and likewise a priest who accepted upon himself the matters of priesthood except for one thing, and likewise a Levite who accepted upon himself the matters of the Levites except for one thing, they are not accepted, as it is stated: “He among the sons of Aaron that offers the blood of the peace offerings…” [Leviticus 7:33]. When the priests do the will of the Omnipresent, what is written about them? “I have given it as their portion of My fire offerings” [Leviticus 6:10]; and when they do not do the will of the Omnipresent, what is written about them? “Who is there even among you that would shut the doors” [Malachi 1:10]. “And all of them who retracted are never accepted,” etc. [This is] in the Tosefta of tractate Demai, in the chapter [Rashi identifies by the words] “Rice in its place is permitted … in the ḥalla of Antioch.”
tosafot:a1.1: And all of them who retracted, etc.: Rashi explained in the first chapter of Avoda Zara (7a) that this refers to robbers and amei ha’aretz who turned from wickedness to good. This is puzzling: why should they not be accepted? That would imply there is no way to make an am ha’aretz [a ḥaver] who accepts upon himself the matters of ḥaver status. Furthermore, the word “never” implies that they had already accepted once before. Furthermore, Rabbi Yehuda says, “If they retracted in private they are not accepted”: that would mean that if they returned to good in private and not in public they are not accepted; but is this not one who fears Heaven in secret? Rabbeinu Tam says that it refers to the first clause, taught in the Tosefta of Demai, in chapter two: An am ha’aretz who accepted upon himself the matters of ḥaver status, etc.; [the printed text adds in parentheses: a gentile who accepted upon himself the matters of ḥaver status, etc.;] a convert who accepted upon himself the matters of Torah, etc.; a priest who accepted upon himself the priesthood, etc.; a Levite who accepted the service of the Levites, etc. And then it teaches: “And all of them who retracted,” that is, who returned to their old ways and corrupted their deeds, are never accepted, since they could not hold to it. Rabbi Yehuda says: “In private,” that is, if they returned to their old ways in private while in public they are careful about the matters of ḥaver status, they are not accepted, because they deceive people and act only for show. But if they corrupted their deeds entirely, even in public, they are accepted when they repent, because when they return, they return completely.
gershom:a1.1: And all of them who retracted: the wife of a ḥaver who married an am ha’aretz, and the daughter of a ḥaver, and the slave of a ḥaver [as in the baraita at the end of 30b], who now wish to be ḥaverim again: they are not accepted.
gershom:a2.1: If they retracted in private: and not in public, they are not accepted.
rashi:a2.1: They performed their matters in private: so that they did not desecrate the name of Heaven in public; they are accepted.
tosafot:a2.1: There are those who say: if they performed their matters in private: that is, we recognized in them at first, before they returned to their old ways, that they practiced the matters of ḥaver status even in private; then they are accepted when they repent. But if we never recognized that they performed the matters of ḥaver status except in public, while in private they were not careful, they are not accepted, because they deceive people.
gershom:a3.1: There are those who say: if they performed their matters in private. That is, if in private they were not particular about pure foods, they are accepted, since it did not become known to the public that they did not keep pure foods; therefore they are accepted, for they seem to be in their presumptive status as they were at first.
rashi:a3.1: Like that pair: Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa.
rashi:a4.1: Tax collector [gabbai]: one appointed by the king to collect taxes from Jews.
gershom:a4.1: And became a gabbai: a customs collector.
rashi:a5.1: Needed him for a matter: the Sages needed him, to ask him about halakhot.
gershom:a6.1: Needed him for a matter: to ask him a matter of halakha, because he was a great scholar. And some say he was ill and they needed to visit him. (The note ends with an abbreviation whose meaning is unclear.)
rashi:a5.2: Tied for them: he tied together and prepared four hundred for them.
gershom:a7.1: Tied for them four hundred takhtekei: he adorned four hundred chairs for them.
rashi:a5.4: Go to your importance: let him go to his importance, the importance he chose for himself, to be a customs collector, and we will not go to him.
gershom:a8.1: Go to your importance, go to your former state: that is, since he has already been a tax collector, let him go to his importance and to his former occupation, and we will not go to him.
rashi:a5.5: I have repented: of tax collecting.
rashi:a7.1: And he may inspect his consecrated animals: if he has peace offerings in his house and a blemish developed in them, he may see whether it is permanent, redeem them and make them non-sacred.
rashi:a7.2: His tithes: an animal tithe in which a blemish developed.
rashi:a7.3: And he may ask about his pure foods: he himself, if he is expert in the halakhot, may ask himself about his pure foods if a doubt arose about them, and he need not go to another Sage.
rashi:a8.1: Except for his own: a priest may not inspect the blemish of his own firstborns and permit them.
rashi:a8.2: And is one trusted: to permit a firstborn, even someone else’s? But we learned below in chapter Kol Pesulei HaMukdashin (Bekhorot 36b): A firstborn whose eye was blinded or whose foreleg was severed may be slaughtered on the word of three members of the synagogue.
rashi:a8.3: Rather, with three: and the priest who owns the firstborn is one of them.
rashi:a8.4: And are they suspect: all of them, on his account?
gershom:a9.1: Are they suspect: even regarding their own?
rashi:a8.5: But didn’t we learn: in Yevamot.
rashi:a8.6: She performed refusal or ḥalitza: a woman, before the Sage; he may marry her, and he is not suspected of having permitted her on that condition.
rashi:a8.7: Because he is a court: that is, he was not there alone; rather, a court of three was there.
rashi:a9.1: As Rav Ḥisda said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said, by a single expert: in tractate Nedarim, chapter Na’ara HaMeorasa (Nedarim 78a).
gershom:a10.1: As Rav Ḥisda said, by a single expert: he inspects firstborns. Here too we are dealing with a single [expert], who does not inspect his own because of suspicion.
rashi:a10.1: And he may inspect his consecrated animals: and he is not suspected of calling a temporary blemish permanent, for why would he lie? If he wanted to make them non-sacred, he could do so in a permitted way: ask a Sage and open with regret, [saying] the consecration was a mistake, “I consecrated it in error.” But with a firstborn, which he did not consecrate, since it is sacred from the womb, one cannot say this, and so he is suspect.
gershom:a11.1: And he may inspect his consecrated animals: and he is trusted to say it is a permanent blemish, and he may redeem them, even according to Shmuel.
gershom:a12.1: Since he could ask about them: before a Sage, and he can say, “I did not consecrate this one but another,” so that it was not consecrated; therefore he is trusted to permit it.
rashi:a11.1: And his tithes: for he is not suspected of calling a temporary blemish permanent, since had he wanted, he could have acted in a permitted way at the outset, before he tithed his herd.
rashi:a11.2: Inflict a blemish on all of them: for they are not yet sacred, so it is not like inflicting a blemish on consecrated animals; and afterward he tithes, for animal tithe takes effect on a blemished animal, as it is written: “He shall not inquire whether it is good or bad” (Leviticus 27:33). Therefore he is not suspect.
gershom:a13.1: And tithes, to permit them by their blemish, so that they need not be eaten within the wall [of Jerusalem]: since, if he wanted, he could inflict a blemish on his whole herd, and the tithe would be blemished of itself.
rashi:a12.1: And he may ask about his pure foods: he is not suspected of calling impure pure, for if they are impure, what does he lose? They are fit for him in his days of impurity. And this speaks of non-sacred food, for impure teruma is not fit for him even in his days of impurity.
tosafot:a12.1: Since they are fit for him in his days of impurity: This is puzzling: what of impure teruma, which is not fit for him? Would he then not be trusted? And likewise in all other matters of the prohibited and the permitted. And it is said explicitly at the beginning of chapter HaDar (Eruvin 63a): A young Torah scholar may examine for himself [and rely on his own ruling].
gershom:a14.1: And he may ask about his pure foods: members of his household may ask him if a doubt of impurity arose in his pure foods, and he is trusted to permit them, since even when impure they are fit for him to eat in his days of impurity. We say: why would he lie? And he is trusted.
gershom:a15.1: We will return to you, Ad Kama [the end of chapter 4].
rashi:a14.1: MISHNA: All disqualified consecrated animals: consecrated animals in which a blemish developed.
rashi:a14.2: Their benefit belongs to the Temple: if they are sold at a high price, the benefit is the Temple’s. And in the Gemara it is all explained.
rashi:a14.3: In the itliz: in the market, where many buy and it sells at a high price.
rashi:a14.4: And weighed by the litra: in the way butchers sell non-sacred meat.
gershom:a16.1: Itliz: in the butchers’ market. Since their benefit belongs to the Temple, one may treat their [value] lightly, selling them in the market and weighing them, for in the market they sell at a high price and there will be profit for the Temple. But a firstborn, since the benefit of its value is the owner’s, one may not treat lightly. And although one does not weigh it against the litra itself, one may weigh firstborn meat against a litra of non-sacred meat; that is “a portion against a portion.”
rashi:a15.1: The firstborn and the tithe: if they are sold at a high price, [the benefit is the owner’s].
rashi:a15.2: Their benefit belongs to the owner: the benefit of a firstborn is the priest’s; he sells the meat to whomever he wishes, since the meat of a firstborn may be eaten by anyone, and the priest takes its money; and it calls the priest the owner of the firstborn. And with the tithe, the benefit of selling it at a high price is its Israelite owner’s. And for the sake of ordinary people’s benefit we do not treat consecrated things lightly, conducting ourselves with them as with non-sacred animals by selling them in the market. Rather, [it is sold] in his house, even though people will not rush to buy it as much; and it is not weighed by the litra but sold by estimate; and if he loses, it does not concern us.
tosafot:a15.1: MISHNA: Except for the firstborn and the tithe, whose benefit belongs to the owner: Although it gives the reason that their benefit belongs to the owner, it must be by Torah law, as is evident in the first chapter of Temura (8a) and at the end of Ḥelek (Sanhedrin 112b), regarding the idolatrous city, where it expounds “your animals”: those that are eaten as your animals, excluding the firstborn and the tithe, which are not eaten as your animals, as we learned: All disqualified consecrated animals are sold in the market except for the firstborn and the tithe. And perhaps it is derived from a verse that one does not treat with disrespect something whose benefit does not go to the Temple.
rashi:a16.1: And one may weigh a portion against a portion with a firstborn: if he has a piece of non-sacred meat that was weighed by the litra, he may weigh firstborn meat against it.
rashi:b2.1: GEMARA: Rather, before its redemption: and the money goes to the Temple.
rashi:b2.2: They are slaughtered: [asked] in astonishment. How can he sell it, making it non-sacred, after slaughter?
rashi:b2.3: But it requires standing and valuation: for a consecrated animal is redeemed only while alive, as it is written: “Then he shall set the animal before the priest, and the priest shall value it” (Leviticus 27:11–12).
rashi:b3.1: This works out well according to the one who says: in the last chapter of Temura (32b), that consecrated items of the altar were not included in standing and valuation; one can then establish that they are redeemed and sold after slaughter.
gershom:b1.1: This works out well according to the one who says consecrated items of the altar were not included in standing and valuation: it teaches that they are slaughtered even before their redemption, and afterward he can redeem them, and they do not require standing.
gershom:b2.1: But according to the one who says they were [included], what is there to say? How can he redeem them after slaughter?
rashi:b4.1: To the initial [redemption]: when the owners first redeem them from the Temple, there is benefit to the Temple; if you permit him to sell it in the market after redemption, he redeems it for more.
gershom:b3.1: To the initial: for at the time of their redemption there is benefit to the Temple, since he adds to their redemption [price] in return for being permitted to sell them in the market.
rashi:b6.1: Whose benefit belongs to the owner: for no money at all is given to the Temple for a firstborn or an animal tithe.
rashi:b7.1: You shall not redeem: “But the firstborn of an ox, or the firstborn of a sheep, or the firstborn of a goat, you shall not redeem” (Numbers 18:17). This implies that the owners do not redeem it, but it may be sold to others once it comes into the priest’s hand.
rashi:b7.2: It shall not be redeemed: “then both it and that for which it is substituted shall be holy; it shall not be redeemed” [Leviticus 27:33]. And it is not sold, for we derive “it shall not be redeemed” here from “it shall not be redeemed” [stated of dedicated property], as is explained below in this discussion.
gershom:b4.1: With the tithe too, “it shall not be redeemed,” and it is not sold. This is derived from dedicated property [ḥaramim], where it is written: “it shall not be sold and it shall not be redeemed” [Leviticus 27:28]: just as there, sale goes with it, so too here, sale goes with it.
rashi:b8.1: And he resolved it in the morning from a baraita: he answered it at early dawn from a baraita. Below it explains which baraita, and he answered it thus: here, [in] the mishna, it is about an animal tithe, etc.
gershom:b5.1: And he resolved it in the morning: at dawn, from the baraita [cited] below. Here in the mishna, for it implies that a tithe is not sold in the market, but in his house it is sold, after redemption and after slaughter.
tosafot:b8.1: With an animal tithe of orphans, etc.: Even according to Rava, who permits [selling] an adult’s by inclusion, Rav Sheshet needed to establish it as orphans’, because he understood the mishna to mean without inclusion, like the disqualified consecrated animals in the market.
gershom:b6.1: We are dealing with an animal tithe of orphans, and because of returning a lost item: so that they would not lose, they permitted it; but for an adult, no.
rashi:b8.2: Returning a lost item: for they cannot eat it all, and it will spoil; and it speaks of a blemished tithe.
rashi:b8.3: They touched upon it: to permit it.
rashi:b9.1: Sarseih: his attendant. [The printed Gemara reads “Rabbi Idi”; the Davidson English has “Rav Idi.”]
gershom:b7.1: Sarseih: his attendant; and some say, his interpreter.
gershom:b8.1: He heard it from him: that we are dealing with a tithe of orphans.
rashi:b9.2: He said it in the study hall: this resolution.
rashi:b9.3: The one who stung: whoever stung and bit me by not saying it in my name, let the scorpion sting him: [that is,] a ban of excommunication.
gershom:b9.1: Who stung: that is, who stung me by not wishing to say the halakha in my name.
gershom:b11.1: To dwell in two worlds together [is impossible]. Rather, this is [what they said], “move”: that is, when one says a halakha in his name, they move in this world, and his lips move in the World to Come.
rashi:b10.1: Dovevot: they move; and it is a pleasure for him, for it is as though he were alive.
rashi:b11.1: A pile [komer] of grapes: which one gathers into one vessel for seven or eight days, so that they press on one another and ripen.
gershom:b12.1: Like a pile of grapes: when they begin to be trodden; as soon as one touches it, it murmurs: the lees give out a sound.
rashi:b12.1: What is the baraita: that we mentioned above, “and he resolved it from a baraita.”
gershom:b13.1: What is the baraita: that we mentioned, “and he resolved it from a baraita.”
rashi:b12.2: He includes it in its fat: for it is forbidden to sell the meat, only the fat, the hide and the sinews; he sells and includes in them the price of the meat, selling him the hide and the sinews dearly, for as much as the whole is worth, and gives him the meat as a gift.
tosafot:b12.1: He includes it in its fat: for it is forbidden to sell the meat, but [one may sell] the fat, the hide and the sinews. One can infer from here that even according to the one who forbids below (Bekhorot 32b) registering a gentile [as a partner] in a firstborn, its fat at least is permitted, since it is regarded like the hide, because it is forbidden to a Jew to eat. However, the fat of the sinew, which is not forbidden by Torah law, may be forbidden. But the halakha follows Rabbi Akiva, who permits [this] to a gentile even for the meat, as is explained below.
gershom:b14.1: He includes it in its hide: he sells him the hide so dearly that the value of the meat is included in it, and likewise in its fat, its sinew and its horns, which may be sold, since they are not food. By inference, the tithe of an adult [may not be sold even by inclusion].
rashi:b13.1: What is it saying: first it teaches “one may sell it,” which implies in its usual way, and then it teaches “he includes it.”
rashi:b14.1: Of an adult: one who is not an orphan.
rashi:b14.2: One who buys a lulav: a person may buy in the Sabbatical Year, from an am ha’aretz, produce picked in the Sabbatical Year, because [the lulav] is of the sixth year that entered the Sabbatical Year, and all trees follow the budding, except for the etrog. And he may not buy an etrog in the Sabbatical Year, even though it budded in the sixth, because for an etrog we follow the picking, and it is Sabbatical-Year produce; and one does not hand the money of Sabbatical-Year produce to an am ha’aretz, who trades with it and does not remove it at the time of removal, when it has ceased [from the field] for the wild animals.
gershom:b15.1: A lulav in the Sabbatical Year: may be sold, because it is not fruit.
gershom:b16.1: An etrog as a gift: for he may not sell fruit.
rashi:b16.1: There the matter is not evident: because its price is low, and it is not noticeable that he included them in the lulav. But here, even by inclusion it is evident that he is selling the meat, for it is known that a hide does not sell for such a high price.
gershom:b17.1: There, with inclusion of the etrog, the matter is not evident that he is selling him an etrog, because the price of an etrog is only small, and it is not part of the lulav itself, so the inclusion is not noticeable at all. But here, when he sells him an animal’s hide for the price of meat and the price of hide, it is evident that he is selling him meat by inclusion. Therefore for an adult, even by inclusion, no.
rashi:b17.1: If so: that it all teaches a single case.
rashi:b17.2: Twice: why do I need “animal tithe” that the baraita teaches [twice]?
tosafot:b17.1: In brief: Tosafot list places where the Gemara objects in the same way to a repeated word: Bava Metzia 2a (“this one says, I found it”: “but it teaches ‘this and this’”), Nedarim 4b (“forbidden, forbidden, why do I need it?”), Sanhedrin 3a (“three, three, why do I need it?”), Sanhedrin 8a (on zimmun and the blessing of zimmun with three), Mo’ed Katan 22b (“for joy and for distress, thirty days”) and Bava Batra 104a (“I sell you, I sell you, why twice?”). They ask why in several other places the Gemara says the text “is merely explaining” and does not object to the repetition: Ḥullin 16b (a knife stuck in a wall: “its slaughter is valid”), Ḥullin 98a (pure eggs boiled with impure ones: “forbidden”), Ḥullin 113a (a pure fish salted with an impure one: “permitted”), Bava Kamma 98b (one gave to craftsmen and they damaged it: “liable to pay”) and Gittin 42b (“all my property is given to so-and-so” and “so-and-so my slave”: “they have not acquired”). They answer that in the places where the Gemara objects “why twice?”, it is not as plausible to say “it is merely explaining” as it is in the places where it does not object. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:b18.1: Rava said: If so, as Abaye answered, that an animal tithe of orphans [a printed note suggests reading: is dealt with in the manner of the latter clause, “one who sells it includes it”], why does the baraita say “animal tithe,” “animal tithe,” twice? Rather, Rava said, etc.
rashi:b18.1: Then both it and its substitute: this is written of animal tithe, and from this “it shall not be redeemed” we derive that it is not sold. Therefore, when the verse forbids selling it, it forbids it in the same way as making a substitute.
rashi:b19.1: When does it make a substitute? While alive: so too, when is it not redeemed? The Torah said this only while it is alive; but after slaughter it may be sold.
gershom:b19.1: When is it not redeemed: [that is,] not sold.
rashi:b20.1: And the Sages decreed after slaughter on account of before slaughter: as was taught above: it is not sold, neither alive nor slaughtered.
rashi:b20.2: An item that is appraised: sold while alive, such as the meat, for the whole worth of an animal lies only in the meat; [for this] the Sages decreed after slaughter.
gershom:b20.1: An item that is appraised while alive: that is the meat, for a person appraises while it is alive how much the firstborn [so the text; the discussion is of the tithe] is worth. The Sages decreed that after slaughter it is not sold, on account of before slaughter, when it is forbidden.
